newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - May 8.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - May 8.

text.p: Twins' outback ordeal: Aboriginal trackers found teenage Nelson stowaway twins in remote far north Queensland on Wednesday, ending an ordeal described by a policeman as a "remarkable story of human survival". Page 1.

Coalition's free kids' health pledge falters: The Coalition promise of free healthcare for children under six appeared to be in tatters on Wednesday night after doctors failed to win an increase in the government subsidy offer of $32.50 a visit, and said that many parents would have to pay extra. Page 1.

Morgan bought rugs with ATN money, says Mallard: The spending of NZ First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan is back in the spotlight with an allegation that he bought three Turkish rugs using money intended for Maori television. Page 1.
Morgan goes on TV to defend 'perks': NZ First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan allows the cameras access to his private life in a television show tonight. Page 1.
Inquiry into police computer systems: Parliament's justice and law reform select committee will hold an inquiry into the problem-stricken computer systems used by police. Page 2.

Bolger stresses stance on Germany: New Zealand did not support Germany's bid for a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council, but that decision was not anti-German, Prime Minister Jim Bolger said on Wednesday. Page 2.
Rent on state houses to rise: Rent on some state houses will rise more than $100 a week when a rent freeze is lifted on July 1. Page 2.

Dunne stays firm on tax-cut deferral: United NZ MP Peter Dunne proved himself Parliament's only truly reliable member on Wednesday night when he voted against the government's plan to defer a $1 billiion tax cut scheduled for July. Page 2.

Migrant fraud report not ready -- Bradford: Immigration Minister Max Bradford has said he will not issue an interim report on an investigation into fraud involving immigrants from Bangladesh, despite a request from a parliamentary committee. Page 2.
Policies aim to cut time out of work: Reducing the time people were unemployed would be a key aim of proposed employment policies, Employment Minister Peter McCardle said on Wednesday. Page 2.
No date for Peters appeal: No date has been set in the High Court at Wellington for Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters's appeal against a ruling in a defamation case last year. Page 7.
Time-bomb spectre for banks: Banks faced huge costs dealing with the "Millennium Timebomb" before it goes off on January 1, 2000, KPMG partner Andrew Dinsdale said on Wednesday. Page 17.

Brash halts easing of monetary conditions: Reserve Bank governor Don Brash halted a softening in monetary conditions after saying the bank was still considering recent weak economic data, analysts said on Wednesday.

Clear boss quits after three and a half years at helm: Pugnacious Clear Communications boss Andrew Makin on Wednesday announced he was leaving after three and a half years in the post, characteristically using the occasion to throw a few jabs at the government and Telecom. Page 17.

Coalition's $5b plan won't mean fiscal expansion -- DMG: The Coalition's planned $5 billion extra spending in the next three years will not mean a "fiscal expansion" by the government, relative to the size of the economy, according to Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. Page 17.
Kiwis may gain airport stake: Infratil NZ shareholders look set to be offered an exposure to the operator of newly privatised Perth International Airport through a rights issue. Page 17.
PepsiCo to announce float details today: International food conglomerate PepsiCo will announce details today of its float of its New Zealand KFC and Pizza Hutt fast food businesses. Page 17.
